questions.q: Why do ions in the same trapped-ion chain have 'all-to-all' connectivity?
options: The ions are physically wired together with microscopic conductors
Every ion in the chain participates in the chain's shared vibrational (motional) modes, so a two-qubit gate can couple any two ions through that shared motion, not just adjacent ones
All-to-all connectivity is a software routing feature added by the control system, unrelated to the physics of the chain
Trapped-ion qubits don't actually have two-qubit gates, so connectivity doesn't apply
questions.explain: Because the whole chain shares collective motional modes through Coulomb coupling, any two ions -- not just neighbors -- can be coupled via that shared motion, which is the physical basis of all-to-all connectivity within one chain.

questions.q: What problem does a superconducting chip face that a single trapped-ion chain generally does not?
options: Needing to cool the qubits before any computation can begin
Needing a vacuum chamber to hold the qubits in place
Needing SWAP gates to move quantum information between non-adjacent qubits before a two-qubit gate can be applied, since each qubit is wired only to a fixed set of physical neighbors
Needing lasers to perform any gate operation at all
questions.explain: Superconducting qubits are wired to fixed physical neighbors, so interacting non-adjacent qubits requires inserting SWAP gates to route information across the chip -- overhead a trapped-ion chain's all-to-all connectivity avoids for ions in the same trap.

questions.q: What is the main practical benefit of avoiding SWAP-routing overhead on a trapped-ion chain?
options: It eliminates the need for laser cooling entirely
Circuits with long-range or irregular connectivity patterns can often be compiled with fewer total gates, which reduces the error accumulated before the computation finishes
It makes every trapped-ion gate faster than every superconducting gate
It allows unlimited numbers of ions to be added to a single chain with no downside
questions.explain: Fewer gates generally means less accumulated error, since every gate carries some chance of error -- the connectivity advantage shows up as reduced circuit depth for algorithms that don't match a simple nearest-neighbor layout, not as faster individual gates or unlimited scaling.

questions.q: What limits how long a single trapped-ion chain can practically grow while keeping good gate fidelity?
options: As more ions are added, the chain's vibrational modes become more numerous and closely spaced, making it harder for a laser to cleanly address one mode without disturbing others
Trapped-ion chains have no practical length limit at all
Longer chains require more electrons to be removed from each ion
The limit is purely a software constraint with no physical cause
questions.explain: This 'motional mode crowding' is a real physical scaling bottleneck: longer chains have more closely spaced vibrational modes, making clean laser addressing progressively harder and degrading gate fidelity and speed.

questions.q: What are ion shuttling and photonic interconnects used for?
options: Replacing lasers entirely as the mechanism for performing single-qubit gates
Removing the need for a vacuum chamber in trapped-ion systems
Connecting multiple smaller ion traps together so the architecture can scale past what one chain's motional modes can support
Cooling ions down to their motional ground state before any gates are run
questions.explain: Since a single chain's all-to-all connectivity doesn't scale indefinitely due to motional mode crowding, larger systems connect multiple traps via ion shuttling (physically moving ions between zones) or photonic links (entangling ions in separate traps via photons) -- both reintroducing some routing-style overhead.
